Consulting Framework Business Strategy Product Strategy Go To Market Trading Dollars for Dimes (And Why You Should) Aditya Raj 3 min read · Oct 9, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share Why the scariest thing in business isn’t losing to a rival , it’s deliberately killing your own best-selling product. In early 2007, the iPod wasn’t just a product. It was a culture. It was the white earbuds hanging out of every pocket on the subway. It was the silhouette ads plastered across entire city blocks. Most importantly for Apple, it was nearly 50 percent of the company’s total revenue. It was a golden goose that laid platinum eggs. So when Steve Jobs stood on a stage in San Francisco that January and announced a product that would render the iPod completely obsolete, conventional corporate logic dictated that he was out of his mind. Why build a phone with a built-in music player when selling standalone music players was currently printing billions? Because Jobs knew a uncomfortable truth that most company executives spend their entire careers running away from: If you don’t cannibalize yourself, someone else will gladly do it for you. Press enter or click to view image in full size Photo by Hassan Pasha on Unsplash The Art of Self-Sabotage In the world of management consulting, we call this Cannibalization. Stripped of the boardroom jargon, cannibalization is simply what happens when a company launches a new product that steals sales, customers, or profit margins from its own existing lineup. Imagine you own a cozy neighborhood bakery. Your signature $5 blueberry muffin is a legend. People line up around the block for it. Then, hoping to capture the health-conscious crowd, you introduce a $4 low-sugar bran muffin. If ten new people walk in the door to buy the bran muffin, congratulations: you’ve grown your business. But if ten of your regular blueberry loyalists switch to the bran muffin instead, you haven’t grown anything. You’ve spent money developing, baking, and marketing a new item just to make $1 less per customer. You just cannibalized your own revenue. Trading Dollars for Dimes Not all cannibalization is created equal. In fact, it usually falls into two distinct buckets: the catastrophic kind, and the deliberate kind. Unintentional Cannibalization (Trading Dollars for Dimes): This is the nightmare scenario. A company introduces a lower-margin item or a cheaper alternative, expecting it to attract a brand-new audience. Instead, existing high-paying customers migrate down. Think of a luxury fashion house releasing a cheap diffusion line, only to discover their high-net-worth clients stop buying the $2,000 handbags because the $200 canvas totes made the brand feel common. Strategic Cannibalization (Defending the Fortress): This is the Apple playbook. You knowingly sacrifice a profitable current product because you see where the world is going. When Netflix transitioned from mailing physical DVDs to streaming videos online, they actively killed their most profitable division. Wall Street hated it at first. Subscribers threw a fit. But if Netflix had tried to protect its DVD business, Spotify, YouTube, and Amazon would have eaten their market share alive anyway. The Fear of the Second Act Why is this so hard for most companies to execute? Because human psychology hates letting go of a sure thing. When a product is winning, every incentive inside an organization is aligned to protect it. Product managers want to optimize it. Sales teams want to keep pitching it. CFOs want to keep milking its high margins. Building something that might kill your main revenue driver feels like setting fire to your own house just to see if the fire department is paying attention. But markets don’t care about your historical profit margins. They care about what’s next. If your new product is taking away sales from your old product, it hurts. But if a competitor’s product takes away sales from your old product, it’s fatal. The next time you see a company launch something that seems to undermine their biggest hit, don’t assume they’ve lost their minds. They might just be serving themselves lunch — before the rest of the world decides to take a bite.
